Team is the home of a music release. The plan, the files, the money, the dates and the people in one place, built for artists, managers, labels and the partners who work releases with them. It is free to use, and on Pro, TeamMate does the admin for you.

TeamMate is AI inside Team. It reads the whole release, keeps the plan current, chases what is missing, drafts what is next, updates the sheet and the one-sheet, and briefs the partner. It changes things only where it is safe to, asks you before anything that touches money, dates or a partner, and shows its work.
Do I have to move everything into Team?

No. Team works alongside the tools you already use. On Pro, Connectors read from Dropbox, Drive, Slack, Gmail, Sheets, Notion and more, and write back. Nothing to migrate, nothing to rip out, no new habits to learn.
Can my manager, label and distributor use it with me?

Yes. One release, each person with their part of it. Invite anyone as a collaborator on Free, with unlimited collaborators and workspaces. When one person moves something, the people it touches find out without anyone writing an email.
Is my data used to train AI?

Never. TeamMate reads your release to help you run it, and for nothing else. Neither Team nor its model providers train on your data, every connection is permissioned and revocable in a click, and everything you build is portable and yours to keep.

Assets is the creative library for the release. Artwork, audio, video, documents and links in one place, versioned so the final is always the final, and shareable so no one sends a zip again.
The creative lives in ten places.

The master's in Dropbox, the artwork's in Drive, the video's in a WeTransfer that expired, and the "final" everyone is using is three versions old. Assets pulls every creative file for a release into one library, with the version that is actually final front and centre.
Every bounce and every cut is kept, with who approved which. The final is unambiguous, and last month's version is still there if you need it.
Share a link, not a 4GB zip.
Send a single asset or the whole library, with the access you choose. Press, partners and DSPs get what they need and nothing expires.
No expiry. No zip. Revoke in a click.
Assets attach to the tasks and dates that use them, so the artwork is where the timeline needs it, not in someone's inbox. Deliverables land in the library as tasks get done.
It knows what is in the library and what is not, so "did the final artwork ever land?" has an answer, and missing assets get flagged before they bite.

Running at scale means stricter requirements. Team is built to meet them, with the controls and paperwork procurement teams expect.
Does TeamMate train on my data?

No. TeamMate uses your connected data to answer your questions and do work for your release. We do not train models on it, and neither do our providers. Your data is never pooled with other customers.
Who on my team can see my data?
Only the people you invite, at the access level you set. Role-based controls let you give the right people the whole picture while limiting everyone else to their slice.
Can I disconnect a tool or delete my data?
Any time. Every connection is revocable in one click, and when you disconnect a tool or delete your data, it is removed from Team. Everything you build stays portable and yours to keep.
How are my connected accounts protected?
Connectors are made through each provider's official, permissioned access, and the credentials are held in a dedicated secrets vault. Team only ever reads the scopes you have granted.
Your data is encrypted in transit and at rest with a reputable cloud provider. Enterprise plans can discuss data residency options. Request our security documentation for the full detail.

We started Team because the most important work in music, getting a release out into the world, still runs on a mess of tools, threads and one person's memory. We think it deserves a home.
Black and white, in the studio. Documentary.
Every release is a small operation.

A dozen tools. Twice as many hands. Masters in one folder, approvals buried in a thread, the budget in a sheet, the plan in someone's head. The context that decides whether a release goes well lives everywhere, and nowhere at once.
The tools were never the problem.
The gaps between them were. And somehow one person is expected to hold all of it together, until they take a week off and it turns out they were the system.
So we built the home of the release.

One place that already knows what a release is, works with the tools you have, and does the admin so nothing falls through the cracks and nothing lives in one person's head. We are building the operating system for music releases, starting at the moment everything converges.
You shouldn't have to leave them to get organised. Team works alongside what you already use.
Not yours, and not the one person who remembers everything until they take a week off.

We started Team because getting a release out still runs on a mess of tools, threads and one person's memory. Here is why we built it, what we believe, and who we are building it with.
Product and company building. Operator across TuneCore and Believe.

Kedar spent his career inside the machinery of independent music, first at TuneCore and then at Believe, watching releases succeed or fail on the strength of the coordination around them rather than the music itself.

He started Team to give every release a proper home. He leads product and the company, and built and shipped the live platform with the first customers on a fraction of what most platforms raise to get to a first version.
He still runs releases on Team himself, which is where most of the roadmap comes from.
Go-to-market, operations and technical product leadership.
Jake runs go-to-market and operations, and leads the technical side of the product, including TeamMate, the AI that does the admin.

His background is music-industry operations: the deadlines, the deliveries, the partners and the spreadsheets that hold a release together. He has read more rollout reports than anyone should, and it shows in how Team thinks about a release week.
